stories.title: Is circular financing in AI a problem?
points: Over half the money invested in AI firms in 2021–25 came from other AI firms, central-bank researchers found.
Lucent and Nortel lent to their own customers in the 1990s telecom boom, then lost both loans and sales.
OpenAI is backing Oracle’s data-centre build with $300bn of business it hasn’t yet raised.
stories.why: Part of AI’s booming sales is the industry funding its own demand.
stories.other: The researchers also see sound reasons: suppliers know their customers best, and buyers lock in scarce chips. Warning sign, or sensible financing?

stories.title: Trading AI compute like oil
points: CME Group plans futures on rental rates for Nvidia’s H100 and B200 chips, out to 36 months.
H100 rents hit $8 an hour in early 2024, then fell below $2 in late 2025.
Yet most new futures never draw lasting volume, writes Marc Rubinstein.
stories.why: A traded price for compute would show whether the AI boom is paying off.
stories.other: A GPU-hour isn’t standard: chips age fast and rival indexes disagree. Can a market run by a few giants ever be deep?

stories.title: Spence: a ‘pretty big’ shock is possible
points: He says India has by far the highest potential growth of major economies, and the best digital finance.
His worry: AI built on debt, high valuations and concentrated indices; a sentiment shift could tip the US into recession.
Rising US rates lift the dollar, he adds, forcing other countries to raise rates defensively.
stories.why: India’s growth story still rides on global calm.
stories.other: He rules out a catastrophic collapse; a shock is a risk, not a forecast.

stories.title: Insurers pay more for quitting than dying
points: Of ₹6.3 trillion paid in FY25, death claims were just 7%; surrenders took 37% and maturities 35%.
Only 48% of policies last five years, but 71% of those bought online do, writes Dhirendra Kumar.
First-year commissions on savings-linked policies average 25–37% of premium; renewals just 0–5%.
stories.why: For pure protection, the writer backs plain term cover.
stories.other: Insurers say these are savings products, bought for the maturity payout rather than the death benefit.

stories.title: 550mn use UPI; only 62mn invest in funds
points: EY counts over 550 million active UPI users, but only about 62 million mutual fund investors and about 50 million active equity participants.
Many households find investment products complex, volatile or hard to judge, so access alone won’t create lasting investors, EY says.
It proposes a five-layer ‘Wealth Stack’ (access, data, intelligence, advice, trust) and sees 100 million+ new long-term investors by 2035.
stories.why: India built the payment rails; investing needs advice, not just apps.
stories.other: 100 million is EY’s ambition, not a forecast. Could more ‘guidance’ mean more mis-selling?

stories.title: AI’s $2tn assumption: a boom built on debt
points: Apollo’s Torsten Sløk says hyperscaler credit rests on operating cash flow rising from $600bn in 2025 to $2tn in 2030, about 27% a year.
Alphabet’s free cash flow turned negative in April–June; it sold over $50bn of bonds in the first half, including a 100-year bond.
Some debt sits off the books, like Meta’s ~$27bn Hyperion campus, funded through a venture mostly owned by Blue Owl funds.
stories.why: Shares, bonds, private loans and pensions now ride the same AI bet.
stories.other: Unlike 2008’s low-income households, today’s borrowers are among the richest, highest-rated firms ever. Bubble, or big build?

stories.title: Denmark taxes most; oil states the least
points: Denmark collects 45.3% of GDP in tax, over twice the US’s 19.5%; India 18.1%.
Seven of the top 10 are in Europe; oil-rich Libya (1.2%) and Kuwait (1.4%) are lowest.
US federal spending is projected at 23.3% of GDP in 2026, against revenue of 17.5%.
stories.why: A low tax take can mean bigger private bills, or bigger deficits.
stories.other: Tax share isn’t a quality score: oil wealth and weak collection both look ‘low’. What do citizens get for what they pay?

stories.title: China shuts a record 670+ banks in a year
points: Banking entities fell 23% in four years to 3,139 by 2025; almost all closures were rural lenders.
Fitch calls small rural and city banks the system’s weakest part: poor assets, thin capital, weak governance.
Wuhan took over Z-Bank in July, the first such takeover since 2019.
stories.why: Beijing is pruning weak banks before they turn into bank runs.
stories.other: One researcher notes the worst banks were often left out of mergers. Is this a cleanup, or just a reshuffle?
